newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian government vows safe return for prince.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian government vows safe return for prince.

text.p: Cambodia's new government on Monday said it would guarantee the safety of ousted First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh if he returned to Cambodia, but held firm to its position that the prince must face a court upon his return.
It also suggested talks might be possible with Ranariddh if he were found not guilty of charges levelled against him by Cambodian leader Hun Sen.
Second Prime Minister Hun Sen has accused Ranariddh of weapons smuggling and illegally bringing Khmer Rouge guerrillas into Phnom Penh.

"I have talked with Hun Sen already and both of us will cooperate together to protect the safety of the prince when he returns, and he can bring the most intelligent lawyer in the world (with him)," said First Prime Minister Ung Huot, who was appointed earlier this month to replace Ranariddh.
"If the court finds the prince is not guilty, Hun Sen and I accept to hold political and other discussions with Prince Ranariddh," Ung Huot added in a statement he read on local radio.
Ung Huot invited members of the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) to send a delegation to Phnom Penh to review the evidence against Ranariddh.
"Hun Sen told me that (the government) welcomes ASEAN to send a delegation to Cambodia to find out if Prince Ranariddh is not guilty," Ung Huot said.

Hun Sen overthrew Ranariddh, his former partner in Cambodia's coalition government, on July 6 after two days of fighting in the capital. Hun Sen has sought to justify the power grab by levelling the charges against Ranariddh.

ASEAN, which delayed Cambodia's entry into the regional club in the wake of the coup, has said it wants Ranariddh to be allowed to return to participate in elections next year, but Hun Sen has said the prince must face court charges first.
ASEAN has also raised the possibility of informal discussions between all the Cambodian parties, but Hun Sen rejected that proposal last week.
He called any such meetings a "waste of time".
Ung Huot's statement appeared to be a partial softening of that position, opening the door to talks with Ranariddh if he were found not guilty.
"We can talk when Prince Ranariddh returns to Cambodia and lets the court charge him officially," Ung Huot said.
Cambodia's National Assembly has stripped Ranariddh of his parliamentary immunity, paving the way for him to face charges if he returns.
Ranariddh has dismissed the charges against him and is touring Asia to drum up support.
But King Norodom Sihanouk, who still recognises his son Ranariddh as first prime minister, has called the prince's efforts "practically a lost cause".
On Monday, Sihanouk called the prospect of any talks between Ranariddh and the new government "wishful thinking".
He said Ranariddh's opposition forces were "98 percent" wiped out.
In the northwest, a ragged army of his loyalists hold a shrinking pocket of territory around the town of O'Smach near the Thai border.
After pounding the town with mortar and artillery fire at the weekend, Hun Sen's forces entered the town on Monday but had not yet gained control of it, government military officials said.
